XXIII.


The next morning, when Archer got out of the Fall River train, he
emerged upon a steaming midsummer Boston. The streets near the station
were full of the smell of beer and coffee and decaying fruit and a
shirt-sleeved populace moved through them with the intimate abandon of
boarders going down the passage to the bathroom.

Archer found a cab and drove to the Somerset Club for breakfast. Even
the fashionable quarters had the air of untidy domesticity to which
no excess of heat ever degrades the European cities. Care-takers in
calico lounged on the door-steps of the wealthy, and the Common looked
like a pleasure-ground on the morrow of a Masonic picnic. If Archer had
tried to imagine Ellen Olenska in improbable scenes he could not have
called up any into which it was more difficult to fit her than this
heat-prostrated and deserted Boston.

He breakfasted with appetite and method, beginning with a slice of
melon, and studying a morning paper while he waited for his toast
and scrambled eggs. A new sense of energy and activity had possessed
him ever since he had announced to May the night before that he had
business in Boston, and should take the Fall River boat that night and
go on to New York the following evening. It had always been understood
that he would return to town early in the week, and when he got back
from his expedition to Portsmouth a letter from the office, which fate
had conspicuously placed on a corner of the hall table, sufficed to
justify his sudden change of plan. He was even ashamed of the ease
with which the whole thing had been done: it reminded him, for an
uncomfortable moment, of Lawrence Lefferts's masterly contrivances for
securing his freedom. But this did not long trouble him, for he was not
in an analytic mood.

After breakfast he smoked a cigarette and glanced over the Commercial
Advertiser. While he was thus engaged two or three men he knew came in,
and the usual greetings were exchanged: it was the same world after
all, though he had such a queer sense of having slipped through the
meshes of time and space.

He looked at his watch, and finding that it was half-past nine got up
and went into the writing-room. There he wrote a few lines, and ordered
a messenger to take a cab to the Parker House and wait for the answer.
He then sat down behind another newspaper and tried to calculate how
long it would take a cab to get to the Parker House.

"The lady was out, sir," he suddenly heard a waiter's voice at his
elbow; and he stammered: "Out?--" as if it were a word in a strange
language.

He got up and went into the hall. It must be a mistake: she could not
be out at that hour. He flushed with anger at his own stupidity: why
had he not sent the note as soon as he arrived?

He found his hat and stick and went forth into the street. The city had
suddenly become as strange and vast and empty as if he were a traveller
from distant lands. For a moment he stood on the door-step hesitating;
then he decided to go to the Parker House. What if the messenger had
been misinformed, and she were still there?

He started to walk across the Common; and on the first bench, under
a tree, he saw her sitting. She had a grey silk sunshade over her
head--how could he ever have imagined her with a pink one? As he
approached he was struck by her listless attitude: she sat there as
if she had nothing else to do. He saw her drooping profile, and the
knot of hair fastened low in the neck under her dark hat, and the long
wrinkled glove on the hand that held the sunshade. He came a step or
two nearer, and she turned and looked at him.

"Oh"--she said; and for the first time he noticed a startled look on
her face; but in another moment it gave way to a slow smile of wonder
and contentment.

"Oh"--she murmured again, on a different note, as he stood looking down
at her; and without rising she made a place for him on the bench.

"I'm here on business--just got here," Archer explained; and, without
knowing why, he suddenly began to feign astonishment at seeing her.
"But what on earth are you doing in this wilderness?" He had really no
idea what he was saying: he felt as if he were shouting at her across
endless distances, and she might vanish again before he could overtake
her.

"I? Oh, I'm here on business too," she answered, turning her head
toward him so that they were face to face. The words hardly reached
him: he was aware only of her voice, and of the startling fact that not
an echo of it had remained in his memory. He had not even remembered
that it was low-pitched, with a faint roughness on the consonants.

"You do your hair differently," he said, his heart beating as if he had
uttered something irrevocable.

"Differently? No--it's only that I do it as best I can when I'm without
Nastasia."

"Nastasia; but isn't she with you?"

"No; I'm alone. For two days it was not worth while to bring her."

"You're alone--at the Parker House?"

She looked at him with a flash of her old malice. "Does it strike you
as dangerous?"

"No; not dangerous--"

"But unconventional? I see; I suppose it is." She considered a moment.
"I hadn't thought of it, because I've just done something so much more
unconventional." The faint tinge of irony lingered in her eyes. "I've
just refused to take back a sum of money--that belonged to me."

Archer sprang up and moved a step or two away. She had furled her
parasol and sat absently drawing patterns on the gravel. Presently he
came back and stood before her.

"Some one--has come here to meet you?"

"Yes."

"With this offer?"

She nodded.

"And you refused--because of the conditions?"

"I refused," she said after a moment.

He sat down by her again. "What were the conditions?"

"Oh, they were not onerous: just to sit at the head of his table now
and then."

There was another interval of silence. Archer's heart had slammed
itself shut in the queer way it had, and he sat vainly groping for a
word.

"He wants you back--at any price?"

"Well--a considerable price. At least the sum is considerable for me."

He paused again, beating about the question he felt he must put.

"It was to meet him here that you came?"

She stared, and then burst into a laugh. "Meet him--my husband? _Here_?
At this season he's always at Cowes or Baden."

"He sent some one?"

"Yes."

"With a letter?"

She shook her head. "No; just a message. He never writes. I don't think
I've had more than one letter from him." The allusion brought the
colour to her cheek, and it reflected itself in Archer's vivid blush.

"Why does he never write?"

"Why should he? What does one have secretaries for?"

The young man's blush deepened. She had pronounced the word as if it
had no more significance than any other in her vocabulary. For a moment
it was on the tip of his tongue to ask: "Did he send his secretary,
then?" But the remembrance of Count Olenski's only letter to his wife
was too present to him. He paused again, and then took another plunge.

"And the person?"--

"The emissary? The emissary," Madame Olenska rejoined, still smiling,
"might, for all I care, have left already; but he has insisted on
waiting till this evening ... in case ... on the chance ..."

"And you came out here to think the chance over?"

"I came out to get a breath of air. The hotel's too stifling. I'm
taking the afternoon train back to Portsmouth."

They sat silent, not looking at each other, but straight ahead at the
people passing along the path. Finally she turned her eyes again to his
face and said: "You're not changed."

He felt like answering: "I was, till I saw you again;" but instead he
stood up abruptly and glanced about him at the untidy sweltering park.

"This is horrible. Why shouldn't we go out a little on the bay? There's
a breeze, and it will be cooler. We might take the steamboat down to
Point Arley." She glanced up at him hesitatingly and he went on: "On
a Monday morning there won't be anybody on the boat. My train doesn't
leave till evening: I'm going back to New York. Why shouldn't we?" he
insisted, looking down at her; and suddenly he broke out: "Haven't we
done all we could?"

"Oh"--she murmured again. She stood up and reopened her sunshade,
glancing about her as if to take counsel of the scene, and assure
herself of the impossibility of remaining in it. Then her eyes returned
to his face. "You mustn't say things like that to me," she said.

"I'll say anything you like; or nothing. I won't open my mouth unless
you tell me to. What harm can it do to anybody? All I want is to listen
to you," he stammered.

She drew out a little gold-faced watch on an enamelled chain. "Oh,
don't calculate," he broke out; "give me the day! I want to get you
away from that man. At what time was he coming?"

Her colour rose again. "At eleven."

"Then you must come at once."

"You needn't be afraid--if I don't come."

"Nor you either--if you do. I swear I only want to hear about you, to
know what you've been doing. It's a hundred years since we've met--it
may be another hundred before we meet again."

She still wavered, her anxious eyes on his face. "Why didn't you come
down to the beach to fetch me, the day I was at Granny's?" she asked.

"Because you didn't look round--because you didn't know I was there.
I swore I wouldn't unless you looked round." He laughed as the
childishness of the confession struck him.

"But I didn't look round on purpose."

"On purpose?"

"I knew you were there; when you drove in I recognised the ponies. So I
went down to the beach."

"To get away from me as far as you could?"

She repeated in a low voice: "To get away from you as far as I could."

He laughed out again, this time in boyish satisfaction. "Well, you see
it's no use. I may as well tell you," he added, "that the business I
came here for was just to find you. But, look here, we must start or we
shall miss our boat."

"Our boat?" She frowned perplexedly, and then smiled. "Oh, but I must
go back to the hotel first: I must leave a note--"

"As many notes as you please. You can write here." He drew out a
note-case and one of the new stylographic pens. "I've even got an
envelope--you see how everything's predestined! There--steady the thing
on your knee, and I'll get the pen going in a second. They have to be
humoured; wait--" He banged the hand that held the pen against the back
of the bench. "It's like jerking down the mercury in a thermometer:
just a trick. Now try--"

She laughed, and bending over the sheet of paper which he had laid on
his note-case, began to write. Archer walked away a few steps, staring
with radiant unseeing eyes at the passersby, who, in their turn, paused
to stare at the unwonted sight of a fashionably-dressed lady writing a
note on her knee on a bench in the Common.

Madame Olenska slipped the sheet into the envelope, wrote a name on it,
and put it into her pocket. Then she too stood up.

They walked back toward Beacon Street, and near the club Archer caught
sight of the plush-lined "herdic" which had carried his note to the
Parker House, and whose driver was reposing from this effort by bathing
his brow at the corner hydrant.

"I told you everything was predestined! Here's a cab for us. You
see!" They laughed, astonished at the miracle of picking up a public
conveyance at that hour, and in that unlikely spot, in a city where
cab-stands were still a "foreign" novelty.

Archer, looking at his watch, saw that there was time to drive to
the Parker House before going to the steamboat landing. They rattled
through the hot streets and drew up at the door of the hotel.

Archer held out his hand for the letter. "Shall I take it in?" he
asked; but Madame Olenska, shaking her head, sprang out and disappeared
through the glazed doors. It was barely half-past ten; but what if the
emissary, impatient for her reply, and not knowing how else to employ
his time, were already seated among the travellers with cooling drinks
at their elbows of whom Archer had caught a glimpse as she went in?

He waited, pacing up and down before the herdic. A Sicilian youth with
eyes like Nastasia's offered to shine his boots, and an Irish matron
to sell him peaches; and every few moments the doors opened to let out
hot men with straw hats tilted far back, who glanced at him as they
went by. He marvelled that the door should open so often, and that all
the people it let out should look so like each other, and so like all
the other hot men who, at that hour, through the length and breadth of
the land, were passing continuously in and out of the swinging doors of
hotels.

And then, suddenly, came a face that he could not relate to the other
faces. He caught but a flash of it, for his pacings had carried him
to the farthest point of his beat, and it was in turning back to the
hotel that he saw, in a group of typical countenances--the lank and
weary, the round and surprised, the lantern-jawed and mild--this other
face that was so many more things at once, and things so different. It
was that of a young man, pale too, and half-extinguished by the heat,
or worry, or both, but somehow, quicker, vivider, more conscious; or
perhaps seeming so because he was so different. Archer hung a moment
on a thin thread of memory, but it snapped and floated off with the
disappearing face--apparently that of some foreign business man,
looking doubly foreign in such a setting. He vanished in the stream of
passersby, and Archer resumed his patrol.

He did not care to be seen watch in hand within view of the hotel, and
his unaided reckoning of the lapse of time led him to conclude that, if
Madame Olenska was so long in reappearing, it could only be because she
had met the emissary and been waylaid by him. At the thought Archer's
apprehension rose to anguish.

"If she doesn't come soon I'll go in and find her," he said.

The doors swung open again and she was at his side. They got into the
herdic, and as it drove off he took out his watch and saw that she had
been absent just three minutes. In the clatter of loose windows that
made talk impossible they bumped over the disjointed cobblestones to
the wharf.


Seated side by side on a bench of the half-empty boat they found that
they had hardly anything to say to each other, or rather that what they
had to say communicated itself best in the blessed silence of their
release and their isolation.

As the paddle-wheels began to turn, and wharves and shipping to recede
through the veil of heat, it seemed to Archer that everything in the
old familiar world of habit was receding also. He longed to ask Madame
Olenska if she did not have the same feeling: the feeling that they
were starting on some long voyage from which they might never return.
But he was afraid to say it, or anything else that might disturb the
delicate balance of her trust in him. In reality he had no wish to
betray that trust. There had been days and nights when the memory of
their kiss had burned and burned on his lips; the day before even, on
the drive to Portsmouth, the thought of her had run through him like
fire; but now that she was beside him, and they were drifting forth
into this unknown world, they seemed to have reached the kind of deeper
nearness that a touch may sunder.

As the boat left the harbour and turned seaward a breeze stirred about
them and the bay broke up into long oily undulations, then into ripples
tipped with spray. The fog of sultriness still hung over the city, but
ahead lay a fresh world of ruffled waters, and distant promontories
with light-houses in the sun. Madame Olenska, leaning back against the
boat-rail, drank in the coolness between parted lips. She had wound a
long veil about her hat, but it left her face uncovered, and Archer
was struck by the tranquil gaiety of her expression. She seemed to
take their adventure as a matter of course, and to be neither in fear
of unexpected encounters, nor (what was worse) unduly elated by their
possibility.

In the bare dining-room of the inn, which he had hoped they would
have to themselves, they found a strident party of innocent-looking
young men and women--school-teachers on a holiday, the landlord told
them--and Archer's heart sank at the idea of having to talk through
their noise.

"This is hopeless--I'll ask for a private room," he said; and Madame
Olenska, without offering any objection, waited while he went in
search of it. The room opened on a long wooden verandah, with the sea
coming in at the windows. It was bare and cool, with a table covered
with a coarse checkered cloth and adorned by a bottle of pickles
and a blueberry pie under a cage. No more guileless-looking _cabinet
particulier_ ever offered its shelter to a clandestine couple: Archer
fancied he saw the sense of its reassurance in the faintly amused smile
with which Madame Olenska sat down opposite to him. A woman who had run
away from her husband--and reputedly with another man--was likely to
have mastered the art of taking things for granted; but something in
the quality of her composure took the edge from his irony. By being so
quiet, so unsurprised and so simple she had managed to brush away the
conventions and make him feel that to seek to be alone was the natural
thing for two old friends who had so much to say to each other....

The next morning, when Archer stepped down from the Fall River train, Boston rose up around him like a kettle left too long to simmer: the air thick, the light white and hard, the whole city sweating through its clothes. Near the station the smells struck first—beer yeasting sour in open-door saloons, coffee burned and re-brewed, fruit gone soft in barrels and carts, the sweet rot of bruised skins. Men in shirtsleeves moved with the unselfconscious sprawl of people who share hallways and wash-basins; the clatter of wheels on stones and the metallic cough of a distant streetcar seemed to scrape at his temples. Even the sound had heat in it—flat, relentless, without the softening hush of trees.

He took a cab to the Somerset Club and ordered breakfast as if order itself could keep his mind from running ahead. He began with melon—cool, faintly musky, the knife passing through it with a wet whisper—then waited for toast and scrambled eggs, letting the paper lie open before him while his attention kept darting to the door, to the clock, to the way the waiters’ shoes slapped the floor. In the fashionable streets too there was an untidy, domestic air: caretakers in calico stationed on rich doorsteps, the Common looking like the aftermath of a picnic where the music had stopped but the trampled grass still remembered it. It was the kind of city where sound didn’t echo so much as sprawl—voices, harness-rings, a tinny barrel-organ somewhere forcing a tune into the heat.

To imagine Ellen here, in this slackened Boston, felt like trying to set a bright, sharp spice into boiled water: the flavor wouldn’t take. Yet a new energy had been in him since the night before, since he had told May—almost lightly—that he had “business in Boston” and would go on to New York the following evening. He had let the office letter, conveniently placed where fate could wink at him, do the work of explanation. The ease of it made him briefly ashamed; it had the glibness of other men’s contrivances. But he had no patience for looking too closely at himself. He smoked a cigarette, scanned the Commercial Advertiser, exchanged the usual greetings with men he knew, and felt, with a strange lucidity, that he was still inside the same world while somehow having slipped through the net of its hours.

At half-past nine he went to the writing-room and wrote a few lines. The pen scratched, the paper rasped under his hand; the familiar instruments of communication looked suddenly crude, like tools meant for coarser work than what he was trying to do. He ordered a messenger to take a cab to the Parker House and wait for the answer, then sat with another newspaper spread before him and began to calculate—absurdly—how long a cab would take.

“The lady was out, sir,” a waiter said at his elbow.

“Out?” Archer repeated, and the word tasted foreign in his mouth, as though he had never learned its meaning in the dialect of his own life.

He rose, went into the hall, found hat and stick, and walked out as if pushed. It could not be true—out at that hour? Why had he not sent the note the moment he arrived? The city, a minute ago familiar, became vast and empty, a place with too much air and not enough direction. He started across the Common toward the Parker House, and the noises thinned under the trees into a softer weave: leaves ticking in a faint stir, a distant hoofbeat, a few voices muffled by shade.

On the first bench under a tree she was sitting.

A grey silk sunshade made a small, disciplined shadow above her head—grey, not pink; he could not imagine now how he had ever dressed her in any brighter color. She sat as if she had nothing else to do, her profile drooping with the heat, her hair knotted low at the nape under her dark hat. The glove on the hand that held the parasol was long and faintly wrinkled, as though the day itself had creased it. The whole attitude was listless, yet contained, like a candle that has learned to burn without flicker.

He came nearer. She turned and looked at him.

“Oh,” she said; and for a second there was a startled sharpness in her face, as if some long-expected sound had been heard at the wrong time. Then it softened into a slow smile of wonder and content, as though she had stepped into a remembered room.

“Oh,” she murmured again, and without rising made a place for him on the bench.

“I’m here on business—just got here,” Archer heard himself explain, and, not knowing why, he began to pretend astonishment at finding her. “But what on earth are you doing in this wilderness?”

The words sounded foolish the moment they were spoken, as if flung across distances too great for speech. He had the sensation that if he did not keep talking she would vanish again into the glare.

“I? Oh, I’m here on business too.” She turned so that they were face to face.

The words hardly reached him as meaning; what reached him was her voice. He had not remembered it at all—low-pitched, with a faint roughness on certain consonants, like the grain in a wooden spoon when it strikes a bowl. Nothing of it had remained with him, as if memory, for all its tyranny, could not translate that particular sound into anything it could keep.

“You do your hair differently,” he said; and his heart thudded as though he had crossed some line.

“Differently? No—it’s only that I do it as best I can when I’m without Nastasia.”

“Nastasia; but isn’t she with you?”

“No; I’m alone. For two days it was not worth while to bring her.”

“You’re alone—at the Parker House?”

A flash of her old malice lit her eyes. “Does it strike you as dangerous?”

“No; not dangerous—”

“But unconventional? I see; I suppose it is.” She considered a moment, the parasol’s shadow shifting on her cheek. “I hadn’t thought of it, because I’ve just done something so much more unconventional.”

The irony lingered faintly, like a spice tasted after the mouth has swallowed.

“I’ve just refused to take back a sum of money—that belonged to me.”

He came back and stood before her.

“Some one—has come here to meet you?”

“Yes.”

“With this offer?”

She nodded.

“And you refused—because of the conditions?”

“I refused,” she said after a moment.

He sat down again beside her, as if sitting were the only way to keep his mind from swaying.

“What were the conditions?”

“Oh, they were not onerous: just to sit at the head of his table now and then.”

Silence fell. It had weight; it pressed his ribs in. His heart shut itself in that queer, obstinate way it had, and he groped vainly for words, as if the language he had inherited did not have a vocabulary for the reality before him.

“He wants you back—at any price?”

“Well—a considerable price. At least the sum is considerable for me.”

He paused, circling the question he could not avoid.

“It was to meet him here that you came?”

She stared, then laughed—a quick release. “Meet him—my husband? Here? At this season he’s always at Cowes or Baden.”

“Yes.”

“With a letter?”

She shook her head. “No; just a message. He never writes. I don’t think I’ve had more than one letter from him.”

The mention brought color to her cheek, and Archer felt his own face grow hot, as if the air had thickened again.

“Why does he never write?”

“Why should he? What does one have secretaries for?”

She said it as if it were an innocent word, emptied of its history. Archer felt the old story—known, unspoken—rise like bitterness at the back of his throat. For a moment the question was on his tongue, but the memory of that one letter Count Olenski had written was too present; he swallowed the impulse and asked instead, carefully:

“And the person—”

“The emissary? The emissary,” she repeated, still smiling, “might, for all I care, have left already; but he has insisted on waiting till this evening… in case… on the chance…”

“And you came out here to think the chance over?”

“I came out to get a breath of air. The hotel’s too stifling. I’m taking the afternoon train back to Portsmouth.”

They sat looking straight ahead at the passing figures. The Common’s sounds went on—the far-off creak of a cart, a child’s high call, the dry percussion of shoes—yet around them there was a pocket of hush, as if the leaves above had decided to shelter this particular conversation.

Finally she turned her eyes to his face. “You’re not changed.”

He wanted to answer: I was, till I saw you again. Instead he stood abruptly and looked about at the sweltering park, at the trampled grass and the hot shimmer beyond the trees.

“This is horrible,” he said. “Why shouldn’t we go out a little on the bay? There’s a breeze; it will be cooler. We might take the steamboat down to Point Arley.”

She glanced up at him, hesitating, and he hurried on, as if speed could keep the world from catching them. “On a Monday morning there won’t be anybody on the boat. “Oh,” she murmured again—on the same note of reluctant yielding.

She rose, opened her sunshade, and looked around as if to consult the scene and confirm the impossibility of staying in it. Then her gaze returned to him.

She drew out a little gold-faced watch on an enamelled chain.

She wavered, her anxious eyes searching his. “Why didn’t you come down to the beach to fetch me, the day I was at Granny’s?” she asked.

She repeated, low and exact, as if quoting from the only language she trusted: “To get away from you as far as I could.”

He banged the hand holding the pen against the back of the bench, like a cook knocking a stubborn bottle to start the pour. “It’s like jerking down the mercury in a thermometer—just a trick. Now try—”

She laughed, bending over the paper laid on the note-case. Archer walked a few steps away, staring with radiant, unseeing eyes at passersby who slowed to stare in their turn at the sight of a fashionably dressed lady writing a note on her knee in the Common. The scene had the innocent absurdity of something out of place, like a fine porcelain dish set down on a park bench.

She slipped the sheet into the envelope, wrote a name on it, and put it into her pocket. Then she stood up.

They walked back toward Beacon Street. Near the club Archer caught sight of the plush-lined herdic that had carried his note to the Parker House. Its driver, having performed this exertion, was bathing his brow at a hydrant as if the city itself had wrung him out.

Madame Olenska shook her head, sprang out, and vanished through the glazed doors.

It was barely half-past ten. Yet Archer’s mind filled the hotel at once with the emissary, seated among travellers with sweating glasses at their elbows, waiting for her with the patience of someone used to being obeyed. Archer began to pace before the herdic, the cobbles jolting the soles of his shoes at each turn. A Sicilian boy with eyes like Nastasia’s offered to shine his boots; an Irish matron thrust peaches toward him, their skins warm and faintly furry, the fruit-scent rising when she shifted the basket. Every few moments the doors opened and hot men in straw hats came out, glancing at him as they passed. It astonished him how often the door swung, and how alike the faces were—lank and weary, round and startled, lantern-jawed and mild—repeating themselves as if stamped from one mould by the day’s oppressive heat and the country’s habit of moving in crowds.

Then, in the stream, a different face flashed—pale too, dulled by heat or worry, but quicker, more conscious, more various, as if several expressions lived in it at once. Archer’s memory caught for an instant on a thin thread and then lost it; the face was gone, doubly foreign in that setting, and the thread snapped and drifted away.

He resumed his patrol, unwilling to stand watch in hand within view of the doors. His sense of time, unaided, became a torment. If she stayed so long, it could only be because the emissary had found her and was holding her with words, with pressure, with whatever vocabulary power uses when it means to be obeyed.

“If she doesn’t come soon I’ll go in and find her,” he said aloud.

The doors swung, and she was suddenly at his side.

They got into the herdic. As it jolted forward Archer pulled out his watch and saw she had been gone three minutes.

The windows clattered loose in their frames, making talk impossible; the city’s hard noises battered at them until the wharf came into view and the water lay beyond like a promise. On the half-empty boat they sat side by side on a bench and found they had almost nothing to say—or rather, what they had to say went better unspoken, passing between them in the relief of being away from walls, away from eyes, away from the thick, listening air of rooms.

As the paddle-wheels began to turn and the wharves and shipping slid backward through the veil of heat, Archer felt the familiar world of habit receding too, as if all the old arrangements were being gently unmoored. He longed to ask her if she felt it: that they were setting out on a voyage from which they might never return. But he was afraid of jarring something delicate in her trust. In truth he had no wish to betray it. There had been nights when the memory of their kiss had burned on his lips; even the day before, driving to Portsmouth, the thought of her had run through him like fire. Now that she sat beside him and the boat bore them out into an unknown stretch of day, the nearness had changed: it was deeper, quieter, like a heat held under a lid. A touch might break it.

The boat turned seaward and a breeze began to move around them. The bay, at first an oily undulation, broke into ripples tipped with spray. Behind them Boston remained under its sultry fog, but ahead lay ruffled water, distant promontories, a lighthouse bright in the sun. The soundscape changed with the air: the steady slap and churn of the paddles, the hiss of water, the rigging’s faint clink, the wind’s thin singing in the rails. Archer felt his mind ease under it, as if the right kind of sound could rinse the day clean.

Madame Olenska leaned back against the rail and drank in the coolness between parted lips. A long veil was wound about her hat, but her face was uncovered, and he was struck by the tranquil gaiety in her expression. She seemed to accept their adventure as a matter of course—neither frightened of unexpected encounters nor, worse, feverishly exalted by the possibility of them. That composure—so unforced, so unadvertised—made the world’s rules seem, for the moment, like a dialect one could step out of without apology.

At the inn where Archer had hoped they would be alone, the dining-room was filled with a strident party of innocent-looking young men and women. Their laughter rang too loudly against the bare boards; forks clinked, chairs scraped, voices rose and fell like a bad band practicing the same refrain. The landlord, proud of his information, told Archer they were school-teachers on a holiday.

Archer’s heart sank. “This is hopeless—I’ll ask for a private room,” he said.

Madame Olenska waited without objection, as if she had long ago learned how to move through the world without wasting strength on what could not be changed.

The room he found opened on a long wooden verandah, with the sea coming in at the windows. It was bare and cool. A coarse checkered cloth covered the table; a bottle of pickles stood like a greenish sentinel; and under a little cage a blueberry pie waited, its dark fruit showing through the crust’s cracks, the faint, homely perfume of baked sugar and berries rising even in that spare place. No more guileless-looking cabinet particulier had ever offered shelter to a clandestine couple. Archer fancied he saw Madame Olenska register the reassurance of its simplicity in the faintly amused smile with which she sat opposite him.

A woman who had run away from her husband—and reputedly with another man—was likely to have mastered the art of taking things for granted. Yet the quiet, unsurprised simplicity of her manner blunted his irony. By being so calm, so unastonished, she brushed away the conventions; and he felt, with a sudden tenderness, that to seek to be alone might be the most natural thing in the world for two old friends who had so much to say—if only there existed a language in which it could safely be said.
